about: A design document as a contract between three kinds of content, rather than a layout with prose in it.
Every slot below names its `source`. That word is doing the real work: it is what lets one template
produce three different documents and still be checkable.
derived  The tool computes it from the catalogue and the answers. Deterministic, reproducible, and
the only content a reader can hold the tool responsible for. Never generated.
authored The tool cannot know it and neither can the model: the reader's own taste, market, budget,
team. The document poses the question and leaves the space. Never generated, only asked.
proposed The model writes a first draft from the wizard's answers, and the document marks it as a
draft. This is the category that did not exist before there was a model, and it is the
one that needs the most structure around it.
The temptation, once a model can write, is to call every slot `proposed` and ship a document that
reads beautifully and is wrong in ways nobody can see. The schema exists to make that hard.

derived.note: Reproducible from the dataset and the answers. If two runs differ, that is a bug.

authored.note: The reader's to write. The document asks, in the second person, and leaves room.

proposed.note: Model-drafted. Must carry what it was drafted from and must be marked in the document.

rules: A derived slot may never be generated, and a proposed slot may never be presented as derived.
Every proposed slot carries `because`: the answers and catalogue entries it was drafted from.
Every proposed slot is marked in the printed document, not only in the export.
The document states which slots are drafts on its own first or last page, not in a footnote.
A slot that the model cannot support from its inputs is left as authored. An empty question is
honest; an invented answer is not.
Counts are always derived. Prose is never allowed to state a number a derived slot already holds,
because the two will eventually disagree and the prose will win with the reader.

slots.label: The facts strip
slots.note: Verb, players, count, setting, session length. Positional, and one row per game type.

slots.label: Why anyone plays it
slots.because: The catalogue holds what the game type *is*, not why this instance of it is worth an evening. Those are different claims and only the second one needs the answers.
mustNot: compare to other games by name

example.good: Ten minutes of quiet, then a shape at the end of the corridor that is already closer than it was.
example.bad: An innovative and immersive horror experience that pushes the boundaries of the genre.
example.why: The first says what a minute of play is like and can be checked against the loop below it. The second cannot be checked against anything.

slots.label: How a run starts
slots.because: The catalogue names the entry condition; the answer decides how the player arrives.

slots.label: The device plan
slots.note: The heart of the tool. Every device here is traceable to the answer or the game type that put it there.

slots.label: The order to build it in
slots.note: Sequence is a property of the catalogue, not of the game. The model has no business reordering it.

slots.label: Art direction and references
slots.because: The tool has no images and no taste model, but the mood answer plus the genre is a real constraint, and a first draft of 'cold, low contrast, one warm light source' is more useful than a blank field.
mustNot: name a specific artist or studio
slots.note: Must be labelled as a suggestion in the printed document.

slots.label: Type and colour in use
slots.because: There is no right answer to infer. A model asked for one would invent a palette that looks like every other palette, and the reader would paste it in.
slots.prompt: Which faces and which three colours, and where does each one appear?

slots.label: Audio and sound design
slots.because: Mood and genre are real constraints on a soundscape — dread wants silence with one recurring cue, a arena wants a bed — and the tool has no audio in it at all. A first draft that names the recurring cue is worth more than a blank field, as long as it is marked.

slots.label: Level design and pacing
slots.because: The answers constrain this more than any other prose slot: a shrinking zone, four players and rooms-and-corridors already decide a great deal about pacing, and the model's job is to say it out loud.
mustNot: describe a specific map layout as decided

slots.label: Market, audience and monetisation
slots.because: This is the reader's business, their platform, and their call. A model that answers it is writing fiction that will be quoted in a meeting.
slots.prompt: Who is this for, on which platform, and how does it make money — or not?

slots.label: Build time and scope budget
slots.because: Depends on who is building it, which the tool does not know and must not guess at.
slots.prompt: How long, with how many people, and what gets cut first?

slots.label: Which answer put which device here
slots.note: The Ledger's whole reason to exist. Becomes more important, not less, once prose is in the document: it is the only part a reader can audit.

slots.label: Which sections are drafts
slots.from: the set of slots whose source is 'proposed'
slots.note: Computed from the template, so it cannot fall out of date the way a hand-maintained list would.

brief.note: One page to get a yes. Only two proposed slots appear, which is why it stays a page.

sprint.note: Everything needed to build, in the order it is built. The AI slots that appear here are the ones that help a builder place a device.

ledger.note: Every slot, plus who said so. With a model in the loop this stops being the audit view and becomes the default one.

why: The derived slots are the model's context, and generating a hook before the device plan exists means
writing a hook about a game whose shape is not yet known. It also means the numbers in the prose
Passing the resolved plan in as context is what makes the prose specific. It is the difference
between 'a tense chase' and 'ten minutes of quiet, then a shape at the end of a corridor'.
generation.onFailure: leave the slot authored and print the question
generation.whyLow: The invented sentence is the failure mode, and every step up in temperature buys fluency with plausibility.

gates.check: A proposed slot's text contains no digit that a derived slot already states.
gates.because: Two sources of truth for one number will disagree, and the prose is the one a reader remembers.

gates.check: Every proposed slot has a non-empty `because` naming the slots and answers it used.
gates.because: An unattributable paragraph is the thing this template exists to prevent.

gates.check: Every proposed slot appears in provenance.draft_marker, and the marker is rendered.
gates.because: A reader who cannot tell a draft from a decision will treat it as a decision.

gates.check: Every proposed slot is within maxWords, or reports its overflow.
gates.because: A model asked for 45 words writes 90. A page that overflows is a layout bug the model caused.

gates.check: No proposed slot contains a phrase from its mustNot list.
gates.because: Cheap, blunt, and catches the specific claims that are most damaging — a named competitor, an invented figure, a promised asset count.

gates.check: No authored slot has content unless a human put it there.
gates.because: The one gate that has to be absolute. An authored slot filled by the model is a person's opinion being written for them.

pitch.what_it_is.text: Atmosphere-driven survival: a hunting threat stalks players while they try to escape or hold out.

pitch.hook.text: Ten minutes of quiet, then a shape at the end of the corridor that is already closer than it was.

direction.type_and_colour.prompt: Which faces and which three colours, and where does each one appear?

market.audience.prompt: Who is this for, on which platform, and how does it make money — or not?
